title: Participle clauses
tagline: Drop the subject and the conjunction — a single participle carries the whole clause.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations (participle clauses for reason and time)
Reading & Use of English Part 7 — multiple matching: dense texts thick with reduced clauses
Writing Part 2 — stories and reviews: fluent, economical narrative
Speaking Part 2 — describing photos and events without strings of 'and' and 'because'
why: Participle clauses let a C1 writer pack a reason, a time relationship or extra information into a sentence with only one subject and no conjunction. Reading & Use of English texts are full of them, and examiners expect candidates to produce them, not just recognise them, in the Writing paper. The form itself is simple; the skill is knowing which participle carries which meaning, and never leaving one with no logical subject to attach to.

diagrams.title: From full clause to participle clause

before.text: Because she had trained for months, Sofia felt ready for the marathon.

after.text: Having trained for months, Sofia felt ready for the marathon.

steps: Check that both clauses share the same subject (she = Sofia).
Drop the conjunction and the repeated subject, and turn the verb into a participle: Having trained shows an action completed before the main clause.
Keep the participle clause next to the noun it belongs to, so the meaning stays clear.

rows.label: Pattern
cells: participle clause + main clause, same doer
participle clause + main clause, different doer

rows.label: Problem
cells: none — 'I' did the walking and the seeing
'the accident' cannot walk — the sentence is illogical

rows.label: Fix
cells: While I was walking home, I saw the accident.

head: Participle
Meaning / time
Example
rows: Waiting for the bus, Liam checked his phone.
Not knowing the address, we asked a stranger.
Written in 1848, the novel still feels modern.
Having revised for weeks, Nadia felt confident.
Having been warned twice, he finally listened.
With the deadline approaching, the team worked late.
time or condition, passive, subject omitted
When asked about the delay, she apologised.

use.point: Replacing a reason or cause clause

examples.text: Having missed the bus twice that week, Mateo decided to leave home earlier.
examples.note: perfect participle = reason + an action completed before the main clause

examples.text: Not wanting to seem rude, Sofia stayed until the very end of the ceremony.
examples.note: negative present participle = because she didn't want to

examples.text: Feeling unprepared for the debate, Liam asked Miss Vega for an extra day.
examples.note: present participle = reason, simultaneous with the main clause

examples.text: Arriving at the viewpoint just after dawn, they watched the mist lift over the valley.
Having handed in the final draft, Nadia finally allowed herself to relax.
Once collected, the surveys were analysed by the whole class.

use.point: Adding extra information (a reduced relative clause)

examples.text: Students wishing to resit the exam must register by Friday.
The mural, painted by last year's cohort, still covers the entire corridor.
examples.note: = which was painted; non-defining, so it takes commas

examples.text: Anyone caught using a phone during the test will be disqualified.

use.point: With + noun + participle, and clauses of result

examples.text: With so many tourists visiting Cusco in July, hotel prices double.
examples.note: with + noun + -ing: an accompanying circumstance, no conjunction needed

examples.text: The bridge collapsed, leaving the village cut off for three days.
examples.note: -ing clause of result, placed after the main clause

examples.text: With the results confirmed, the team could finally celebrate.

watch_out.wrong: Walking to school, the rain started suddenly.
watch_out.right: Walking to school, I got caught in the rain.
watch_out.why: Dangling participle — 'the rain' cannot be the one walking; the participle must share its subject with the main clause.

watch_out.wrong: Having finish the report, she sent it to her tutor.
watch_out.right: Having finished the report, she sent it to her tutor.
watch_out.why: The perfect participle needs the past participle after 'having', not the bare infinitive.

watch_out.wrong: Interesting in the topic, Liam read three extra articles.
watch_out.right: Interested in the topic, Liam read three extra articles.
watch_out.why: For feelings, use the -ed form for the person who feels them; -ing describes what causes the feeling.

watch_out.wrong: Build in the 1920s, the theatre has just been restored.
watch_out.right: Built in the 1920s, the theatre has just been restored.
watch_out.why: A passive meaning needs the past participle, not the base form of the verb.

watch_out.wrong: Having been late, the meeting had already started when he had arrived.
watch_out.right: Having arrived late, he found the meeting had already started.
watch_out.why: Keep the timing of the two clauses clear: the perfect participle marks the earlier action, and the main clause should not also repeat 'had'.

watch_out.wrong: When asking about the results, Miss Vega smiled.
watch_out.right: When asked about the results, Miss Vega smiled.
watch_out.why: After when/if/once, a passive meaning needs the past participle, not the -ing form.

dialogue.title: Editing the trip report
dialogue.context: Miss Vega is helping Mateo, Sofia and Nadia tighten their write-ups of the school trip to the Sacred Valley before they go on the class blog.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: This paragraph is accurate, but it's full of short sentences joined with 'and' and 'because'. Can you tighten it up?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: So instead of 'Because we left at five, we reached Ollantaytambo before the crowds', I could write 'Having left at five, we reached Ollantaytambo before the crowds'?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Exactly — and it reads far more fluently.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: What about description? I wrote 'The terraces were built by the Incas and they still look perfect.'

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Try a reduced relative clause: 'Built by the Incas, the terraces still look perfect.'

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Nice. And 'Seen from the top of the ruins, the whole valley looks like a green amphitheatre.'

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: I've got a sentence I'm not sure about: 'Not knowing the altitude would affect us, we ran up the last staircase.'

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: That works well — the participle clause carries the reason without a separate sentence.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: For the ending I want a result clause: 'The bus broke down on the way back, leaving half the class stranded for two hours.'

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Good — an -ing clause of result at the end. Just remember: the subject of the participle has to match the subject of the main clause, or the sentence falls apart.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Like the sentence I deleted: 'Walking along the path, the view was incredible.' The view wasn't walking!

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Precisely. Give it a real subject and the sentence is fixed.

items.sentence: ___ she was close to the deadline, Sofia decided to skip lunch and keep working.
items.why: present participle for an active reason clause: Sofia is the one realising

items.sentence: ___ by torchlight, the ancient manuscript revealed details invisible under normal light.
items.why: passive meaning (the manuscript was examined) needs the past participle

items.sentence: ___ his essay twice, Liam finally felt ready to submit it.
items.why: the perfect participle marks an action completed before the main clause

items.sentence: The hikers, ___ by the sudden storm, took shelter under a rock overhang.
items.why: reduced passive relative clause: who were caught

items.sentence: When ___ about the missing report, the intern admitted she had forgotten to send it.
items.why: after 'when', a passive meaning takes the past participle: when questioned = when she was questioned

items.sentence: ___ so many applicants applying for the scholarship, the school extended the interview period by a week.
items.why: 'with + noun + -ing' introduces an accompanying circumstance without a conjunction

items.sentence: Not ___ how to reach the shrine, the pilgrims asked a local guide for directions.
items.why: negative present participle for reason: because they didn't know

items.sentence: ___ from the article, the quotation had lost its original meaning.
items.why: passive past participle: the quotation was taken out of context

practice.instructions: Complete each sentence with the correct participle form of the verb in brackets.

items.sentence: ___ (finish) the last exercise, Nadia closed her laptop and went outside.
The email, ___ (send) to the wrong address, never reached the headteacher.
___ (not/want) to interrupt the lesson, Liam waited outside the door.
With the whole team ___ (wait) for news, the coach finally announced the result.
When ___ (ask) why she was late, Sofia simply apologised and sat down.
The trail, ___ (close) after the landslide, will reopen next month.
___ (realise) her mistake, Nadia quickly rewrote the paragraph.
Having ___ (check) the figures twice, the accountant signed the report.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first, using the word given. Do not change the word given. Use between two and five words.

items.first: Because she had already read the book, Nadia didn't need to borrow it from the library.
items.second_end: the book, Nadia didn't need to borrow it from the library.

items.first: As he was not sure of the answer, Liam raised his hand cautiously.
items.second_end: of the answer, Liam raised his hand cautiously.

items.first: The flood damaged the bridge, so it had to be closed for repairs.
items.second_end: by the flood, the bridge had to be closed for repairs.

items.first: Since we don't know the final numbers, we can't confirm the budget.
items.second_end: the final numbers, we can't confirm the budget.

items.first: After the judges had checked the scores twice, they announced the winners.
items.second_end: the scores twice, the judges announced the winners.

items.first: As the deadline was approaching, the team began to work extra hours.
items.second_end: the team began to work extra hours.

summary: Drop the conjunction and the subject when both clauses share the same subject, and turn the verb into a participle: Because she was tired → Being tired.
Use the perfect participle (having + past participle) when the action in the participle clause happened before the action in the main clause.
The past participle carries a passive meaning (Built in 1900...); the present participle carries an active one (Building the wall...).
With + noun + participle adds an accompanying circumstance without any conjunction at all.
Always check the subject: if the participle clause and the main clause do not share the same doer, the participle is left dangling — a classic C1 error.
